fetchCuple<TEndpoint>(endpoint, ...args): CuplePromise<TEndpoint["tOutput"]> Defined in: packages/client/src/client.ts:275 Sends one request. It resolves with success, and rejects otherwise: Outcome Rejects with Any other result (a 404, an invalid-body) CupleUnexpectedResponseError No response: unreachable, DNS, CORS CupleTransportError Body is not JSON: proxy HTML, gateway page CupleTransportError (statusCode) options.signal aborted DOMException (name: "AbortError") List the outcomes your code handles, and they resolve as typed values instead: .thenResolveAlso(["invalid-body", "transport-error"]). See CuplePromise. The HTTP status is never interpreted: it is copied onto the result as statusCode, and which result goes with which status is the server's choice, set by apiResponse. A non-JSON body is always an error here — fetchCuple only speaks Cuple's envelope. For downloads, streams and any other custom response, define the route with getRaw/postRaw/… on the server and call it with plain fetch; raw routes are not part of the client API. (Raw request bodies are fine: pass an ArrayBuffer, Blob, Uint8Array or ReadableStream as body.) CupleWithOptions<TParams> = object Defined in: packages/client/src/client.ts:471 Options for client.with(..). The two fields are deliberately separate concerns: data is about the request, key is about the cache. A cookie-authenticated app needs only key; a static API-key client needs only data. Type Parameters​ TParams​ TParams Properties​ finalware?​ optional finalware?: (response) => unknown | Promise<unknown> Defined in: packages/client/src/client.ts:512 Runs after every response this client receives, before it is handed back. For the cross-cutting work that has to happen whether or not a hook is involved: redirecting on an expired session, reporting failures. Throwing from here turns a result into an exception, which is how a redirect works. Returning a value replaces the response; returning nothing keeps it. The types do not follow it. A replaced response still has the endpoint's declared type, because the response type is fixed by the route definition and there is no way to thread a per-client transformation back through it. Reshaping data here will lie to every caller — observe, throw, or narrow by hand at the call site. Parameters​ response​ any Returns​ unknown | Promise<unknown> key?​ optional key?: string | (() => string) Defined in: packages/client/src/client.ts:496 Identifies what middleware injects, for cache integrations. middleware runs per request, so nothing it returns reaches the cache key: two calls that differ only in what it injected would share one entry. This is how a cache tells them apart. Most often that is who the request is for, but it is whatever the middleware actually varies by — a tenant, a locale, an API version. Key what the response depends on, not the injected bytes. A refreshed token is new data but the same identity; a key that moved with it would discard the cache on every refresh and orphan pending invalidations. A getter must be synchronous, since the key is built during render. It is read on each render, so whatever it reads has to live somewhere that re-renders the tree — otherwise pass a plain string and build one client per value. middleware?​ optional middleware?: () => Promise<TParams> | TParams Defined in: packages/client/src/client.ts:477 Runs before every request this client sends; what it returns is merged into the request data, under the per-call options. SSEOptions = object Defined in: builder.ts:109 Properties​ returnOnDisconnect?​ optional returnOnDisconnect?: boolean Defined in: builder.ts:125 Whether to close the handler's generator when the client disconnects. Defaults to true. false is for a generator that ends on its own — one draining a finite job, say, that should finish its work whether or not anyone is still reading. A generator that loops forever must not opt out: nothing will stop it, and after the client is gone it keeps running at full speed, one runaway loop per disconnected request, for the life of the process. A generator that needs to outlive the disconnect only briefly should check disconnectSignal.aborted on each pass and return once it is set. That is also the only way to end one parked on an await rather than a yield, which returnOnDisconnect cannot reach either way.

Option Runs For middleware Before every request; awaited, so it can refresh a token. Data every request needs: headers, a tenant id. key When a cache needs it (a string, or a synchronous getter). Telling caches whose data a response is. See Switching accounts. finalware After every response, before it's handed back. Cross-cutting reactions: redirect on an expired session, report failures. Throwing turns a result into an exception. NOTE: key is what the response depends on (who the user is), not the injected bytes (the token). A refreshed token is the same user. NOTE: finalware can replace the response, but the types don't follow it. Observe or throw; don't reshape. Why it works this way This replaces HTTP interceptors (as in axios). An interceptor adds the auth header out of sight of the types, so a request that misses it is a 401 found at runtime. Here the route's schema makes the header part of the call's type: a call without it doesn't compile, and with() gives you a client whose type says the header is already supplied. with() returns a new client instead of changing the one you have, so one base client can have variants side by side: public, signed in, admin. middleware runs per request because tokens expire. Reading the token when the request is sent means a long-lived client never sends a stale one. key is separate from middleware because a cache needs it synchronously, and middleware is async. It also names who the data belongs to, not the token: a refreshed token is the same user. finalware can replace the response, but the types don't follow. Fixing that would be welcome, but it isn't critical: nothing relies on it.

fetchCuple resolves with success. Anything else rejects: import { fetchCuple } from "@cuple/client"; const { user } = await fetchCuple(client.getUser.get, { params: { id } }); Outcome Rejects with Any other result: a 404, an invalid-body CupleUnexpectedResponseError, with the response No answer: offline, DNS, CORS, a proxy's HTML error page CupleTransportError signal aborted DOMException (AbortError)

When your code has something to do with a failure, list it. It resolves as a typed value instead of rejecting: const res = await fetchCuple(client.createUser.post, { body }).thenResolveAlso([ "invalid-body", ]); // ^? success | invalid-body if (res.result === "invalid-body") showIssues(res.issues); Anything you didn't list still rejects, and goes where unhandled errors go. "transport-error" can be listed like any result, for code that has something to do when the server can't be reached (a form that keeps the user's input). It resolves as { result: "transport-error", statusCode, message }. statusCode is set when something answered, but not in Cuple's format (a gateway page). "abort" can be listed too, for a request you cancel on purpose. It resolves as { result: "abort", statusCode: null, message }.

Method Resolves with .thenResolveAlso([...]) success, plus the listed results .thenResolveOn([...]) exactly the listed results; "success" is not implied .thenResolveAnyResponse() every result the server sent, for code that forwards responses as they are (a proxy, an MCP tool). A network failure or an abort still rejects. .thenResolveAll() everything: every result the server sent, plus transport-error and abort. Only a bug in your own code rejects. const res = await fetchCuple(client.search.get, { query, options: { signal } }).thenResolveAlso([ "abort", ]); if (res.result === "abort") return; // a newer search replaced this one

@cuple/react follows the same rule: useGet gives you success, and { resolveAlso: [...] } lists what the component renders instead. Inside useAction, use thenResolveAlso. Whatever nobody listed goes to the nearest <Boundary>. See Errors. Why it works this way The first client, client.route.get(), worked like fetch: every result resolved, and only a network error threw. Its return type was very complex, and anything built on it had to repeat that type, so fetchCuple takes the route as an argument instead. fetchCuple resolves only success to match useGet. In a component you want the data, and dealing with an error is an enhancement. On its own, resolving everything and unwrapping success on request would read slightly better, but one rule across the client and React is worth more. A failure you list is typed in the return value, with its real shape. A try/catch gives you unknown. "transport-error" and "abort" can be listed like any server result, so handling offline or a cancelled request is the same code as handling any other failure. The lists are chained methods (.thenResolveAlso([...])), not an option of fetchCuple, because of a typing limit.
npm i @cuple/client NOTE: @cuple/client and @cuple/server versions have to match

We need to tell Cuple about the server's location. Every request goes to one path (usually /rpc) and names the route. Routes with .path() are also plain REST endpoints for other clients. // cuple.ts import { createClient } from "@cuple/client"; import type { routes } from "../backend/src/app"; export const client = createClient<typeof routes>({ path: "http://localhost:8080/rpc", });

import { fetchCuple } from "@cuple/client"; async function getPost(id: number) { // Resolves with success; any other result throws. const { post } = await fetchCuple(client.getPost.get, { params: { id } }); return post; } async function findPost(id: number) { // A failure you handle is listed, and typed. const res = await fetchCuple(client.getPost.get, { params: { id } }).thenResolveAlso([ "post-not-found", ]); return res.result === "post-not-found" ? null : res.post; } See Handling results. Why it works this way There's no code generator because type inference does the job: the client's types are inferred from typeof routes, so they're the server's own types. A monorepo, where the client imports them directly, is the intended setup. One RPC path follows from that. The client has only types, and the URL isn't in them (types are erased at runtime anyway). Importing the routes value would bundle the server into the client. Routes without .path() have no URL of their own anyway.

// Server: const routes = { foo: builder.get(/**/), bar: builder.post(/**/), baz: builder.put(/**/), qux: builder.patch(/**/), quux: builder.delete(/**/), }; // Client: await fetchCuple(client.foo.get); await fetchCuple(client.bar.post); await fetchCuple(client.baz.put); await fetchCuple(client.qux.patch); await fetchCuple(client.quux.delete);

Since Cuple doesn't have a code generator, you have to tell the HTTP method in order to build up the fetch request with the right method. It's type-checked so you cannot specify methods other than what the server specifies.

Create combined reads at module level. A combined read's identity is its cache identity; one created during render would never hit the cache. Args must be JSON (numbers, strings, plain objects and arrays): they're the cache key. It owns what it fetches. The calls made through ctx.get are kept as long as the combined read is, whatever their own cache settings. So "load more" fetches one page, never all of them again. Refreshing a route re-runs every combined read that read it. refresh: [client.getOrder] updates loadOrderWithCustomer too. ctx.get shares requests with every other reader: if the list already loaded a customer, the order page doesn't fetch it again. Why it works this way Combining reads is a plain async function, so there's nothing new to learn. During the design, a combined read was going to keep state of its own, such as how many pages were loaded. But a combined read lives in the cache, so whenever the cache dropped it, that state would be lost. So state lives in React (useState, the URL) and is passed in as arguments. The cache should only make things faster, never change what you see.

Nothing is refreshed unless the action names it. List what a write changes. When the server computes one thing from another (property cards counting permits), list both: /** The cache. One per app; plain code (sign-in, SSE handlers) uses it directly. */ export const store = createCupleStore(); /** What each write changes, in one place. Actions name these in `refresh`. */ export const refreshes = { notes: [client.getNotes, client.getNote], contacts: [client.listContacts, client.getContact], }; // Switching accounts re-reads only what depends on the account: every call's // key changed, so each reader reads again under the new one. The previous // account's data is dropped at once (the default `keepOnKeyChange: false`): the // next person at this screen may not be the same person. export function signIn(accountId: AccountId) { signedInAs = accountId; store.refreshKeys(); } // Signing out drops everything: nothing of the account stays in memory. export function signOut() { signedInAs = null; store.clear(); } /** One action per row, so each row has its own pending state. */ function NoteRow(props: { note: { id: number; text: string }; onOpen: (id: number) => void; }) { const remove = useAction( () => fetchCuple(client.deleteNote.delete, { params: { id: props.note.id }, }), // A failed row action shouldn't take the page with it. { refresh: refreshes.notes, config: { errors: { onError: "notify" } } }, ); return (

The rest are dropped, and fetched fresh when next read. So when you delete the note an open pane shows, and close the pane inside the action, the deleted note is never refetched and never 404s. refresh: [...] refreshes every time the function finishes. refresh: { success: [...] } refreshes only for the listed results, as NewTodo above does; the keys are typed from what the function returns.

Errors you handle are results you list with thenResolveAlso, "transport-error" included: typed values in value. Anything else your function throws (a result it didn't list, a network failure it didn't list, a bug) is unhandled, and config.errors.onError decides where it goes: per action, per <Boundary>, or app-wide on the provider: "boundary": the nearest <Boundary>, as a CupleError. The default. "notify": config.errors.notify shows it; the page stays, and the status becomes failed. Errors never end up only in the console. See Errors for all the cases in one app.

When a component moves to another item, give it a key (key={note.id}), or it shows the previous item's result. The state is the latest run's. An earlier run that finishes later still writes and refreshes, but doesn't change what is shown. Steps that must all happen or none belong in one server route. The client can sequence steps, but it can't make them a transaction.

Page numbers don't depend on each other, so Promise.all fetches them in parallel, which matters when a refresh refetches every loaded page. refresh: [client.getNotes] re-runs the combined read: every loaded page is fetched again, and the list stays on screen meanwhile. With cursors, each page's cursor comes from the page before, so the walk is sequential: export const notePages = combine(async (ctx, args: { count: number }) => { const pages = []; let cursor: number | null | undefined; while (cursor !== null && pages.length < args.count) { const page = await ctx.get(client.getNotes, { query: { cursor } }); pages.push(page); cursor = page.nextCursor; } return { notes: pages.flatMap((page) => page.notes), hasMore: cursor !== null }; }); A cursor walk survives deletions: when a note is deleted, a refresh recomputes the cursors, and nothing is skipped. Page numbers shift instead, and the refresh realigns them. Why it works this way An early @cuple/react had a usePages hook, but it was a specific solution for the simplest case, and combine already does what pages need: several reads, one value, refreshed together. So pagination is a recipe with combine, not a hook of its own. A combined read owns the pages it fetched. Without that, each page would follow its own cache settings, so the cache could drop earlier pages while the list is open, even with storeStaleMs: Infinity on the list. The next "load more" would then quietly refetch all of them.

Every behavior is set through one config object, grouped by concern. Going back and forth between screens is instant, without keeping everything for good. maxStoredCalls: 3: of one endpoint, at most the 3 most recent entries nobody reads are kept (one per set of arguments). A search shouldn't keep every keystroke in memory, and a limit is a safer default than none. keepOnKeyChange: false: when the client's key changes (another account signs in), the previous key's data is deleted at once. It can be large, and must not show to the next user. onError: "boundary": an error in an action that nobody handled replaces the nearest <Boundary>'s content with its error view. Setting Default What it does enabled true false keeps nothing once it's unread: data is dropped as soon as the last reader unmounts, and fetched again when read again. Readers mounted at the same time still share one request. The same as freshMs: 0, storeStaleMs: 0: for search boxes, and large data. freshMs 0 How long data counts as fresh after it lands. A component that starts reading cached data (another tab, a reopened panel) shows it at once, and refetches it in the background only if it's stale. 0 always refetches, Infinity never. Fresh data nobody reads is never dropped. A first load is never fetched twice: "coming back" means some component has read this data before. storeStaleMs 5 minutes How long data nobody reads stays in memory once it's stale. The clock starts when it is both stale and unread, whichever comes last. With several readers, the longest wins. The entries a combined read makes through ctx.get are kept as long as the combined read itself, whatever their own settings. maxStoredCalls 3 How many entries of one endpoint (or one combined read) nobody reads are kept, whatever freshMs and storeStaleMs say. Past it, the one unread the longest is dropped. Entries something reads never count, and neither do the entries a cached combined read made. Different args are different entries, so a search keeps its last few queries, not every keystroke. With several readers, the largest wins. keepOnKeyChange false Whether store.refreshKeys() keeps data whose key changed: false deletes it at once, true keeps it like any unread data, so switching back is instant: only when one person owns every account, since the old account's data shows again at once. Every failure is either handled or unhandled. Handled means your code listed it: thenResolveAlso(["invalid-body"]) on a request, resolveAlso: ["note-not-found"] on a read. The store is the cache. Components reach it through <CupleProvider>; plain code uses it directly.

await store.refresh([client.getNotes, client.getNote]); Entries something is reading are refetched, and keep their old data on screen until the new data lands. Entries nobody reads are dropped, and fetched fresh when next read. It resolves when the refetches have landed, and never rejects: a failure goes to whoever reads the data. A network failure during a refresh keeps the old data on screen, and is retried when the browser comes back online.

Start a fetch before anything renders it: <li onMouseEnter={() => store.preload(loadOrderWithCustomer, order.id)}> It never rejects, and a failed preload isn't kept: nobody was waiting for it, so the next read fetches again. In a router loader, call it without returning it (void store.preload(...)), so loading and errors stay with <Boundary> instead of the router. NOTE: A read of { id: 5 } doesn't hit a preload of { id: "5" }. When that happens, the store warns in the console.

The cache doesn't know what your client's middleware sends, so tell it whose data a cache entry is, with a key: let signedInAs: AccountId | null = null; export const client = createClient<typeof routes>({ path: "/rpc" }).with({ // Whose data a call is: each account's calls are cached under its own key. key: () => signedInAs ?? "signed-out", middleware: () => ({ headers: { authorization: signedInAs ? ACCOUNTS[signedInAs].token : "" }, }), }); When the account changes, call store.refreshKeys(): /** The cache. One per app; plain code (sign-in, SSE handlers) uses it directly. */ export const store = createCupleStore(); /** What each write changes, in one place. Actions name these in `refresh`. */ export const refreshes = { notes: [client.getNotes, client.getNote], contacts: [client.listContacts, client.getContact], }; // Switching accounts re-reads only what depends on the account: every call's // key changed, so each reader reads again under the new one. The previous // account's data is dropped at once (the default `keepOnKeyChange: false`): the // next person at this screen may not be the same person. export function signIn(accountId: AccountId) { signedInAs = accountId; store.refreshKeys(); } // Signing out drops everything: nothing of the account stays in memory. export function signOut() { signedInAs = null; store.clear(); } It checks every cache entry's key again: Key unchanged: stays as it is. No request, no re-render. Key changed: its readers read again under the new key, even memoized ones. Cached data for the new key shows at once; anything else loads. The old key's data is deleted at once (cache.keepOnKeyChange: false, the default), so nothing of it can show again. true keeps it like any unread data, so switching back is instant: use it only when one person owns every account, like work and personal inboxes. Combined reads built from a changed call run again; streams reconnect. Wrap it in startTransition to keep the current screen until the new data is ready. Signing out calls store.clear(): nothing of the account stays in memory. Both exist because the right UX differs: refreshKeys() can keep the screen until the new account's data arrives, clear() empties it at once.
store.clear(); Drops everything; readers suspend and fetch again. For sign-out and tests.

Please follow the steps in the comments. import express from "express"; import { z } from "zod"; import { createBuilder, initRpc } from "@cuple/server"; import { apiResponse, success } from "@cuple/server"; const app = express(); const builder = createBuilder(app); // STEP 1: Create builder with the express instance const posts = [ { id: 1, title: "Hi again", content: "This is my second post" }, { id: 2, title: "Hi", content: "This is my first post" }, ]; // STEP 2: Define some request handlers export const routes = { getPosts: builder.get(async () => { return success({ posts }); }), }; // STEP 3: Create the RPC handler (Required to use with @cuple/client) initRpc(app, { path: "/rpc", routes }); app.listen(8080, () => { console.log(`Example app listening on port 8080`); }); Why it works this way Cuple runs on Express because it started there: Express registers the endpoints and parses the JSON bodies. That's history, not a design goal. Supporting other frameworks would be welcome. Until then, being an Express app has a side benefit: logging, CORS, sessions and deployment stay as they are, and Cuple routes sit next to the ones you already have. The routes object exists only for its type. Each builder.get(...) already registers its route on app, so ideally defining a route would be enough. But TypeScript can't collect types from side effects, so the routes have to be gathered into one value. Its type is the contract: the client, the OpenAPI generator and the MCP server all read it, so they can't disagree. It's exported only so the client can import the type. Usually you also export type Routes = typeof routes and the client uses import type. The OpenAPI generator and the MCP server find the variable by name, so they don't need the export. initRpc is needed because the client has no code generator. Without generated code, it doesn't know each route's URL, so it calls every route on one endpoint and names the route in the request. initRpc creates that endpoint, and without it the client can't call anything. It's a separate step because it's simple enough on its own, and because on a platform where one shared endpoint makes no sense (AWS Lambda, if it's ever supported), it wouldn't apply. Every setup supported today needs it. Routes with .path() are still plain REST for other clients.
With @cuple/mcp, AI agents can call your routes as MCP tools. Like OpenAPI, it reads your routes from the TypeScript source. npm i -D @cuple/mcp typescript

// mcp.ts import { serveMcp } from "@cuple/mcp"; serveMcp("./src/routes.ts", "routes", { url: "http://localhost:8080/rpc" }); Then register it with your agent as a command. For example, in Claude Code: claude mcp add my-api -- npx tsx mcp.ts In this example: "routes" is the name of the exported variable that holds your routes, as for generateOpenAPI. Every route becomes a tool, named after the route, e.g. posts.getPost. .meta({ description }) becomes the tool's description. A tool's input is what the route declares: params, query, body and headers, the same as fetchCuple's. Tools call your running server at url, through the RPC endpoint, so routes without .path() work as well. The response is given back as JSON. If it's not success, the tool call is marked as an error. NOTE: serveMcp talks to the agent over stdin and stdout, so don't write logs to stdout in mcp.ts. NOTE: It reads your TypeScript source, so run it where the source is available.

The tools say what each route needs, headers included. With a login route and a route that requires authorization: login: builder .bodySchema(z.strictObject({ email: z.string(), password: z.string() })) .post(async ({ data }) => success({ token: await signIn(data.body) })), listPosts: builder .chain(authLink) // .headersSchema(z.looseObject({ authorization: z.string() })) .get(async () => success({ posts })), listPosts's tool requires headers.authorization, so the agent calls login with the credentials you give it, and sends the token it gets back with the gated calls. There's nothing to configure. NOTE: The token goes through the conversation, like anything the agent reads. Give an agent an account with only the access it needs. TIP: For local testing, accept a dev token that only works in development mode, and give it to the agent. Then it can call gated routes without signing in itself.

createMcpServer takes the same arguments and returns the server without connecting it, for a transport of your own: import { createMcpServer } from "@cuple/mcp"; const server = createMcpServer("./src/routes.ts", "routes", { url: "http://localhost:8080/rpc" }); await server.connect(transport); // any transport from @modelcontextprotocol/sdk Why it works this way MCP is here so AI agents can easily call Cuple endpoints. They're good with HTTP but don't know Cuple's /rpc protocol, and the tools do that part for them. It's early and not well tested yet. Tools call your running server, so an agent gets the same validation, middlewares and auth as your app, and can reach nothing a normal client can't. The route's types are its instructions: an agent learns that listPosts needs authorization the same way it learns it needs params, with no extra setup to keep in sync. Running as a separate process that reads the source is only where it started. An initRpc option that also serves MCP from the app would be simpler. Choosing which routes become tools isn't done yet either.
Adding every routes in one file can be hard to do. Luckily, you don't have to.

const authModule = { login: /*...*/, register: /*...*/, } const postsModule = { getPost: /*...*/, getPosts: /*...*/, createPost: /*...*/, deletePost: /*...*/, } const app = { auth: authModule, posts: postsModule, } export type Routes = typeof app; Deeply nesting modules is also supported.
Cuple lets you do it your way, but if you are unsure here's an example: Usually it make sense to have createSomeModule function that initializes the module with all of its dependencies and routes.

// index.ts const routes = { auth: createAuthModule(db, builder), }; // modules/auth/index.ts export function createAuthModule(db: PrismaClient, builder: Builder) { return { login: builder.post(async ({data}) => { /* login */ }), register: builder.post(async ({data}) => { /* register */ }), // ... }; }

Since Cuple is REST compatible, you can generate an OpenAPI 3.0 spec from your routes. It reads your TypeScript source at build time, so there's nothing to add at runtime. npm i -D @cuple/openapi typescript

// routes.ts export const routes = { getPost: builder .path("/api/posts/:id") .paramsSchema(z.strictObject({ id: z.coerce.number() })) .get(async ({ data }) => { const post = await getPost(data.params.id); if (!post) return apiResponse("post-not-found", 404, { message: "Post not found" }); return success({ post }); }), createPost: builder .meta({ description: "Creates a new blog post" }) .path("/api/posts") .bodySchema(z.strictObject({ title: z.string(), content: z.string() })) .post(async ({ data }) => { return success({ id: 1 }); }), }; // scripts/openapi.ts import { generateOpenAPI } from "@cuple/openapi"; generateOpenAPI("./src/routes.ts", "routes", { tsconfigPath: "./tsconfig.json", info: { title: "Blog API", version: "1.0.0" }, outputFile: "./openapi.json", }); In this example: "routes" is the name of the exported variable that holds your routes. /api/posts/:id becomes /api/posts/{id}. Every possible response is included, grouped by status code, so 404 post-not-found is in the spec as well. .meta({ description }) becomes the operation's description. The operation id is the name of the route, e.g. getPost, or posts.getPost if it's nested. NOTE: Only routes with .path() are included, the others are only reachable through the RPC endpoint. NOTE: generateOpenAPI returns the document as well, so outputFile is optional.

Cuple OpenAPI .path("/posts/:id") path /posts/{id} .get() / .post() / ... operation with that method .paramsSchema(...) path parameters .querySchema(...) query parameters .headersSchema(...) header parameters .bodySchema(...) application/json request body return values responses by status code .meta({ description }) description

@cuple/openapi is built on @cuple/inspect, which you can use directly if you need the route information for something else: import { inspectRoutes } from "@cuple/inspect"; for (const route of inspectRoutes("./src/routes.ts", "routes")) { console.log(route.method.toUpperCase(), route.path.raw); } Why it works this way The spec is generated from the source, because hand-written specs drift from what the handlers return. It's read at build time because return types don't exist at runtime. Passing a file path and a variable name instead of the routes object is a TypeScript compiler API limit: the generator needs the object's type, not its value. Passing routes directly would be better if a way is found. OpenAPI 3.0 is only the first version written. Updating to 3.1 is planned.

The normal handlers give you JSON responses only. You still have access to Request and Response objects, so you can set, for example, custom headers. However, if you need xml, binary, or any other kind of response, you can use raw handlers. builder.getRaw(async ({ req, res, data }) => {/* ... */}) builder.postRaw(async ({ req, res, data }) => {/* ... */}) builder.putRaw(async ({ req, res, data }) => {/* ... */}) builder.patchRaw(async ({ req, res, data }) => {/* ... */}) builder.deleteRaw(async ({ req, res, data }) => {/* ... */})

Use raw handlers when you need: Non-JSON responses (XML, CSV, binary files, downloads) Streaming responses (file streams). For Server-Sent Events, use getSSE. Feature Normal Handlers Raw Handlers Response format JSON only Any format Error handling Automatic Manual Client support @cuple/client, fetch fetch

With normal handlers, if a middleware fails (returns { next: false }), the error response is automatically sent back as JSON. You don’t need to handle it manually. With raw handlers, this automatic behavior is disabled. The data object passed into the raw handler contains both success and error responses of your middlewares. That means you must explicitly send both success and error responses of your middlewares yourself.

builder .path("/test") .middleware(async () => { if (Math.random() < 0.5) { // success case: continue return { next: true, bar: "hey", }; } // failure case: stop execution return { next: false, statusCode: 400, foo: "hello", }; }) .getRaw(async ({ res, data }) => { if (data.next === false) { // middleware blocked -> manual error response res.status(data.statusCode).send(data.foo); } else { // middleware passed -> manual success response res.status(200).send(data.bar); } });

Cuple uses Express under the hood, giving you full access to req and res objects. With raw handlers, all automatic behavior is disabled, allowing you to use Express as designed while benefiting from Cuple's type-safe composition features. Please check express tutorials for more. Why it works this way Raw handlers are separate because a file download or a CSV isn't a typed result. Keeping them apart keeps every other route fully typed, instead of widening all responses to "anything". Middleware failures aren't sent automatically, because a raw route may need to answer an error in its own format (XML, plain text), not JSON. The Cuple client can't call raw routes yet. Supporting them, for example returning a Blob for a download, would be welcome.

Here's a very basic request handler: builder.get(async () => { return { result: 'success' as const, statusCode: 200 as const, message: "Hey!" } }) The builder is the request handler builder that you've created during the installation. The .get sets the final middleware with the appropriate HTTP method. The supported methods are: get, post, put, patch, delete The async () => { /* ... */ } is the function where your controller logic leaves The return type should contain these fields: result: names what happened, e.g. "post-not-found" or "email-taken". It identifies the response, so name the situation, not the status code (not "not-found-error"). statusCode: the HTTP status code, the category of the response. For client-side typing it needs to be const as well.

Adding result and statusCode manually can be noisy. It's advised to create factory methods for common response types like success. success is included in the package: import { success } from '@cuple/server' builder.get(async () => { return success({ message: "Hey!" }) }) A failed schema returns invalid-body, invalid-query, invalid-params or invalid-headers (see Schema validation). For a rule a schema can't check, return the same result with invalidInput, so the client handles both the same way: import { invalidInput } from '@cuple/server' builder.post(async ({ data }) => { if (data.body.password1 !== data.body.password2) return invalidInput("body", [{ code: "custom", path: ["password2"], message: "Passwords do not match.", }]); // ... }) And there's also a generic apiResponse method, so you don't have to keep track the shape of the return type: import { apiResponse } from '@cuple/server' builder.get(async () => { return apiResponse("post-not-found", 404, { message: "This post doesn't exist.", }); }) Example for custom factory method: export function postNotFound(others?: { message: string }) { return apiResponse("post-not-found", 404, { message: others?.message || "This post doesn't exist.", }); }

The first argument is an object containing 3 elements: req: Express' Request object res: Express' Response object data: custom data from the middlewares builder .chain(auth) .bodySchema( z.strictObject({ oldPassword: z.string(), password1: z.string().min(6), password2: z.string().min(6), }), ) .post(async ({ req, res, data }) => { // You can access request object req.body // but you have better, type-safe way to deal with the incoming data data.body.password1 }) Why it works this way A response is a discriminated union, because errors need types too. When the server rejects bad input, the client should get that error with its real shape (the issues), not just a success type and an unknown. So every response is one member of a union like { result: "success", ... } | { result: "invalid-body", ... }, and TypeScript narrows it. The statusCode is there because Cuple deliberately stays on HTTP. A Cuple backend should look like any industry-standard API, so every response carries a real status code. A discriminated union could narrow on statusCode alone, and you can do that. But different outcomes can share a status code: a 404 can mean "no such route" or "no such order". So result identifies the response, and statusCode is its category: generic code (a redirect on any 401) branches on the status, and specific code (showing "this post was deleted") on the result. Handlers return their response instead of calling res.send, because only a returned value is in the handler's type, and so in the client's. A response sent by hand is invisible to both. Returning also reads better than a callback. req and res are still passed in, so that you can do anything Express allows. They're there to help, not to limit what you can do.

Middlewares allow you to reuse logic by handling tasks like validation, access control, or response formatting. They offer several features: Passing data to other middlewares. Preventing further execution based on conditions. Sending responses, so you don't need to handle every case manually. Note: Schema validators are also treated as middlewares.

builder .middleware(async () => { const randomValue = Math.random(); if (randomValue > 0.5) return { next: true, randomValue }; return { next: false, statusCode: 500, message: "Unlucky" }; }) .get(async ({ data }) => { return success({ message: `You won with ${data.randomValue}`, }); }); In this example: If the middleware returns { next: true }, the execution proceeds to the next handler. You can also type-safely add data, as shown with randomValue in data.randomValue If the middleware returns { next: false }, it sends an immediate response, which requires a statusCode. It's recommended to include a result: 'some-error' as const: the client can check res.result instead of res.statusCode, and if it relies on result, every response needs one.

Some middlewares need to use data coming from schema validators. In order to use the data from the schema validation you have to keep the middleware function in the builder code. This, however, prevents you to just move the middleware function out of the builder. To solve this, Cuple introduces a wrapper called link, and you can connect links with each other. .buildLink() Creates a link from a build chain. Use this instead of the final middleware (get, post, ...). .chain(fooLink).chain(barLink) to bring multiple links into the build chain

const authLink = builder .headersSchema( z.looseObject({ authorization: z.string(), }) ) .middleware(async ({ data }) => { if (data.headers.authorization === "foo") return { next: true, }; return { next: false, statusCode: 401 as const, }; }) .buildLink(); const routes = { getAuthedWelcomeMessage: builder .chain(authLink) .get(async () => { return success({ message: "hi" }); }), };
Middlewares can depend on the output of previous middlewares. For example, a role-check middleware might depend on the result of an authentication middleware.

const authLink = builder .middleware(async () => ({ next: true, auth: { userId: 12345 } })) .buildLink(); const adminRoleLink = builder .expectChain<typeof authLink>() .middleware(async ({ data }) => { const user = await getUser(data.auth.userId) if(user.role !== 'admin') { return { next: false, statusCode: 403, message: "This is admin only." } } return { next: true, user } }) .buildLink(); return { someRoute: builder .chain(authLink) .chain(adminRoleLink) .get(async ({ data }) => { return success({ message: `You have access! Good ${data.user.name}` }); }), }; In this example: adminRoleLink depends on the output of authLink.

In more complex applications, middleware may need additional services like a database or external APIs. To keep the code maintainable and testable, it's best to inject these dependencies rather than import them directly. You can achieve this by creating middleware link factories.

function createAuthLink(builder: CupleBuilder) { return builder .middleware(async () => ({ next: true, auth: { userId: 12345 } })) .buildLink() } type AuthLink = ReturnType<typeof createAuthLink> function createAdminRoleLink(builder: CupleBuilder, userRepository: UserRepository) { return builder .expectChain<AuthLink>() .middleware(async ({ data }) => { const user = await getUser(data.auth.userId) if(user.role !== 'admin') { return { next: false, statusCode: 403, message: "Admins only." } } return { next: true, user } }) .buildLink() } function createAdminModule(builder: CupleBuilder, userRepository: UserRepository) { const authLink = createAuthLink(builder); const adminRoleLink = createAdminRoleLink(builder, userRepository); return { someRoute: builder .chain(authLink) .chain(adminRoleLink) .get(async ({ data }) => { return success({ message: `You have access! Good ${data.user.name}` }); }), }; } note: CupleBuilder is an exported type from the index.ts file

Middlewares added with app.use still run before Cuple routes, but their effects aren't in the types. Cuple parses JSON bodies itself, so a middleware that changes normal request handling (rewrites the body, or sends its own response) can break Cuple endpoints. Why it works this way Middlewares return data instead of attaching it to req. req.user set by a middleware is invisible to TypeScript, and a route that forgot the middleware still compiles. Returned data is typed in data, and exists only on routes that use the middleware. next: true | false makes the return a discriminated union, so TypeScript knows which return is data for the next step and which is a response to the client. Links exist so a middleware made of several builder steps, like auth (headersSchema + middleware), can be moved out of the route as one piece.

Instead of returning one response, you can stream events with an async generator. Every yielded object is sent to the client as an event. The supported methods are: getSSE, postSSE, putSSE, patchSSE, deleteSSE

builder .chain(authLink) .getSSE(async function* ({ data, disconnectSignal }) { for await (const event of activityFeed.subscribe(disconnectSignal)) { yield { action: event.action, by: data.account.name }; } }); In this example: Middlewares run before the stream opens. Opening a stream sends the status (200) first, so after that an error can only close the stream. Running auth and validation before it means a rejection is still a normal JSON result with its own status. When the client disconnects, the generator is stopped, and disconnectSignal is aborted.

const stream = await fetchCupleSSE(client.activity.get, {}); for await (const event of stream) { console.log(event.by, event.action); } In React, use useStream. NOTE: By default the generator is stopped when the client disconnects, so a client that navigates away doesn't leave a subscription or a loop running on the server. If your generator ends on its own, and it should finish even without the client, use getSSE(generator, { returnOnDisconnect: false }). Never do this with an endless loop. Why it works this way A stream is an async generator because yield is the closest thing to return: a handler that streams reads like one that responds once, and the yielded type flows to the client. SSE is here because it was low-hanging fruit on plain HTTP. WebSockets are planned. The separate methods (getSSE, postSSE, …) are a typing limit and an ergonomics choice: a streaming handler has a different type from a normal one.

Cuple uses Zod for schema validation. It was choosen because of the good defaults and the great type inference. Within Cuple the ZodIssue is also extended for additional type-safety. You can validate, parse, and convert each part of an HTTP request.

Internally it parses express' req.headers object, so you should use the same naming. Use z.looseObject: every request carries headers you didn't declare (host, user-agent, …), and a strict object would reject them. Successfully parsed result will be added to data.headers. builder .headersSchema(z.looseObject({ authorization: z.string() })) .get(async ({ data }) => { data.headers.authorization // this has a string value });
Currently only json requests are supported. Successfully parsed result will be added to data.body. .bodySchema(z.strictObject({ user: z.strictObject({ name: z.string().min(3), age: z.number() }) }))

Note: Query parameters are always strings! Luckily zod can convert it to number if you use z.coerce.number(). Successfully parsed result will be added to data.query. // For URL query parsing (e.g.: ?somevar=12) .querySchema(z.strictObject({ somevar: z.coerce.number() }))

Note: Path parameters are always strings! Luckily zod can convert it to number if you use z.coerce.number(). Successfully parsed result will be added to data.params. // For URL params parsing .path("/post/:id") .paramsSchema(z.strictObject({ id: z.coerce.number() }))

A failed schema answers with status 422, and the result names the part that failed: invalid-body, invalid-query, invalid-params or invalid-headers. An issue's path is relative to that part. An example response for a body: { result: 'invalid-body', statusCode: 422, message: "We found some incorrect field(s) during validating the form.", issues: [{ path: ["email"] message: 'This field is required.' code: 'invalid_type' }] } To report a rule only the server can check (an email already in use) the same way, return it with invalidInput("body", issues). See Request handlers. Why it works this way Invalid input is a normal result, not a thrown error, and this is why Cuple was started. A thrown error isn't typed. An invalid-body in the response union has typed issues with a path, so the client can type-safely put each message on its field. Zod was the safest choice: fields are required by default and type inference is good. Only the issues needed a small patch, to narrow each path to strings and numbers. No better option is known today.
